# Diagnosing OBD2 Communication Failures on Legacy ECUs

Connecting a modern diagnostic tool to a 2004 Proton GEN2 and receiving nothing but a "connected" status in the app is a classic case of protocol mismatch or hardware handshake failure. The fact that your Torque Pro app indicates a connection while the ECU remains silent suggests the physical layer (UART/ISO-TP) is active, but the application layer negotiation has failed. This often happens when the diagnostic software attempts to query a controller using a standard OBDII (SAE J1979) protocol that the legacy manufacturer never implemented fully.

When you connect an OBD2 device, it typically powers up and sends a broadcast request asking all nodes on the bus to identify themselves. In modern vehicles, this results in a `0x01` PID response containing the ECU family ID. However, older ECUs from brands like Proton often lack full compliance with the SAE J1979 standard. Instead of responding with the standard identification PIDs, they may require manufacturer-specific commands or simply remain silent until a specific service is requested.

The issue isn't necessarily that the ECU is dead; your observation that the Engine Light is on confirms the powertrain control module (PCM) is receiving power and monitoring sensors. The problem lies in how Torque Pro interacts with the device. By default, most diagnostic apps attempt to read standard OBDII PIDs first. If the ECU does not respond to these specific queries within a timeout window, the app might still report "Connected" because the serial port is open, but it cannot retrieve any data streams.

To troubleshoot this, you need to verify whether your scanner supports manufacturer-specific protocols. Many generic OBD2 dongles rely on a single firmware configuration optimized for Toyota or Honda, which may not include the custom communication scripts required for Proton. You can try switching the device's firmware or using a different brand of scanner that explicitly lists support for "Other" or "Legacy" protocols in its settings.

If you are comfortable modifying the Torque Pro configuration, check the `AndroidManifest.xml` or the specific `.tq3` file if you are using custom builds to see if there are alternative protocol handlers enabled. Sometimes, enabling "Raw CAN" mode or switching from ISO-TP to raw UART can yield different results, though this is risky as it bypasses the flow control expected by most ECUs.

Another possibility involves the vehicle's battery state. Older cars often have weak batteries that drop below the threshold needed for stable OBD2 communication once the ignition key is turned to the "ON" position but before the engine starts. The ECU might be in a low-power sleep mode or resetting its internal watchdog timer, causing it to ignore diagnostic requests temporarily. Try disconnecting the battery for a few minutes to reset the ECU's memory, then reconnect and attempt the scan again immediately after turning the ignition on.

Finally, consider that the ECU itself might have entered a "limp home" mode or has corrupted firmware due to age, preventing it from responding to diagnostic queries even when the MIL is active. In such cases, the only resolution is reflashing the ECU with a known good image using a professional flash tool capable of writing raw binary data directly to the ECUs memory map. Until then, generic OBD2 apps will likely remain unable to retrieve live data from this specific unit.
